title: “DO NOT DEPRIVE ONE ANOTHER”: Does This Verse Give a Spouse the Right to Demand Sex?
paragraphs: “DO NOT DEPRIVE ONE ANOTHER”: Does This Verse Give a Spouse the Right to Demand Sex?

What 1 Corinthians 7:5 actually says about sex, marriage, mutuality, consent, temptation—and the devastating damage done when a verse about giving yourself in love becomes a weapon for taking from someone else.
There are Bible verses people run to for comfort.
There are Bible verses people avoid because they bring conviction.

And then there are Bible verses that have been placed into wounded hands, angry arguments, marriage counseling sessions, bedrooms filled with silence, and relationships where one person whispers something like:
“But the Bible says you’re not supposed to deprive me.”
Maybe you have heard it.
Maybe you have said it.

Maybe someone said it to you when you were exhausted, frightened, sick, emotionally shattered, recovering from childbirth, carrying unresolved betrayal, struggling with trauma, or simply not ready for sexual intimacy at that moment.
Maybe the words that were supposed to represent God somehow made you feel as though God Himself had signed someone else’s permission slip to ignore your “no.”
So we need to ask the question carefully.
Does 1 Corinthians 7:5 give a husband or wife a biblical right to demand sex from their spouse?
Read the passage.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 7:5, KJV
Those words are serious.
But before anybody turns them into ammunition, we need to notice something enormously important.
Paul does not begin this discussion with the language of one spouse conquering another.
He begins with mutual responsibility.
The Greek behind “do not deprive one another” is:
μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους
mē apostereite allēlous *
The verb ἀποστερέω — apostereō carries the idea of depriving, defrauding, or withholding what is due.
But then comes a word that changes the atmosphere of the entire sentence:
ἀλλήλους — allēlous
“One another.”
Not “wives, do not deprive your husbands.”
Not “husbands, your wife owes you whatever you demand.”
One another.
Paul deliberately speaks in reciprocal language.
And the surrounding verses make that mutuality even more striking.
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”

Then Paul writes that the wife does not exercise authority over her own body but her husband does—and immediately, without allowing the husband to turn that sentence into unilateral power, Paul reverses the construction:
“Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
—see 1 Corinthians 7:3–4
That symmetry matters.
Especially in the ancient world, it is difficult to miss how remarkable Paul's reciprocal formulation is.
The husband is not presented as a sexual king whose desires become commands.
The wife is not presented as a sexual servant existing to satisfy him.
Nor does Paul reverse the hierarchy and make the husband merely an instrument for the wife’s desires.
He places both spouses under a radical principle of mutual self-giving.
Marriage, in Paul's description, is not:
“Your body belongs to me, therefore I can take.”
It is much closer to:
“I no longer live as though my body exists only for myself, therefore I am called to give myself to you in love.”
Those are profoundly different postures.
One reaches.
The other gives.
One demands.
The other serves.
One asks, “What am I entitled to get from you?”
The other asks, “How can I love you faithfully?”
And that distinction becomes critical when Christians talk about sex.
Because someone can quote a technically real Bible verse while expressing a profoundly un-Christlike heart.
Imagine a spouse trembling.
Imagine tears.
Imagine fear.
Imagine someone freezing because memories of previous abuse have suddenly flooded back.
Imagine someone saying, “Please, not tonight.”
Then imagine the other spouse opening a Bible and saying:
“God says you cannot deprive me.”
Something has gone terribly wrong.
Scripture has stopped being received as the Word that exposes our selfishness and has become a weapon used to enforce someone else's surrender.
That is not what this passage authorizes.

First Corinthians 7 teaches that sexual intimacy matters in marriage. It teaches that persistently withholding intimacy can become spiritually and relationally destructive. It teaches spouses not to use sexual deprivation selfishly or manipulatively. It recognizes sexual temptation as real. It encourages married believers to take seriously the sexual dimension of their covenant.
We should not erase any of that simply because the passage has sometimes been abused.
But neither should we manufacture another teaching Paul never gives:
“Therefore a spouse must submit to sex whenever the other spouse demands it.”
That conclusion does not follow from the text.
In fact, look again at verse 5.
Paul makes an exception for temporary abstinence:
εἰ μήτι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρόν
The crucial expression is ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou.
It means, in essence, by agreement, by mutual consent, or by mutual accord.
The word carries the idea of harmony or agreement—the linguistic family from which English eventually receives “symphony.”
Paul envisions husband and wife communicating and agreeing.
That should immediately challenge any theology of marital sexuality built around coercion.
There is something else we desperately need to recover.
The Bible's vision of marriage cannot be separated from the Bible's vision of love.
Paul—the same apostle writing 1 Corinthians 7—will later tell the Corinthian church:
“Love is patient and kind.”
Love “does not insist on its own way.”
—see 1 Corinthians 13:4–5
Think about that.
The Christian cannot read:
“Do not deprive one another”
and pretend Paul never wrote:
“Love… does not insist on its own way.”
Nor can Christian husbands isolate 1 Corinthians 7 from the terrifyingly beautiful standard of Ephesians 5:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Jesus becomes the model.
And what does Jesus do?
Christ gives Himself.
He lays Himself down.
He loves sacrificially.
He does not teach husbands to imitate domination.
He commands a kind of love modeled after Calvary.
That changes the question.
Instead of:
“How much can I demand because we are married?”
Christian love asks:
“How much of my selfishness am I willing to crucify so that I can love my spouse like Christ?”
That question cuts both ways.
Because sexual manipulation can happen through pressure.
And sexual manipulation can also happen through deliberate withholding.
A spouse can sin by coercing.
A spouse can also weaponize rejection, using intimacy as punishment, leverage, control, humiliation, or retaliation.
Neither reflects Christ.
This passage should therefore convict more than one kind of heart.
It confronts the person who says:
“You owe me, so I don't care how you feel.”
And it confronts the person who says:
“I know intimacy matters deeply to you, but I am going to withhold affection specifically to control you.”
Both can reduce another human being to an instrument.
The Gospel calls us somewhere better.
But we also need compassion here, because not every absence of sexual intimacy is “deprivation” in the manipulative sense.
Sometimes there is illness.
Pain.
Medication.
Hormonal changes.
Pregnancy.
Postpartum recovery.
Grief.
Depression.
Disability.
A demanding season of life.
Sexual dysfunction.
Exhaustion.
Past abuse.
Betrayal.
Fear.
Relationship wounds that have never been repaired.
Sometimes the bedroom is cold because something outside the bedroom is bleeding.
And demanding sex will not heal it.
Sometimes the most intimate thing a husband can do is listen.
Sometimes the most loving thing a wife can do is finally tell the truth about why she has been pulling away.
Sometimes both need to stop pretending everything is fine.
Sometimes repentance is needed.
Sometimes forgiveness.
Sometimes medical help.
Sometimes wise pastoral care.
Sometimes professional counseling.
Sometimes patient rebuilding after betrayal or trauma.
And sometimes the sentence that begins restoration is not:
“You owe me.”
It is:
“Tell me where it hurts.”
That is where this becomes intensely personal.
Because perhaps your marriage does not need another argument about who is technically correct.
Perhaps it needs truth.
Perhaps underneath the sexual conflict is rejection.
Underneath the anger is loneliness.
Underneath the avoidance is fear.
Underneath the demand is insecurity.
Underneath the silence is shame.
Underneath the resentment is an old wound neither of you has had the courage to name.
You can win an argument over 1 Corinthians 7 and still lose the heart sleeping beside you.
And some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You sleep inches apart.
But emotionally?
Miles.
You remember when touching felt safe.
You remember laughing in bed.
You remember when affection wasn't negotiated like a business contract.
Now every rejection feels like judgment.
Every request feels like pressure.
Every silence becomes evidence.
Every night adds another brick to the wall.
And eventually two Christians can lie beside each other while both privately wondering:
How did we get here?
The answer will not be found by ripping one sentence out of Scripture and throwing it across the bed.
Bring Jesus back into the room.
Not merely the name of Jesus.
The character of Jesus.
His patience.
His truth.
His tenderness.
His holiness.
His willingness to confront sin.
His refusal to exploit weakness.
His grace toward broken people.
His sacrificial love.
Because Christian marriage was never supposed to become a competition over who possesses whom.
It is a covenant in which two people learn, imperfectly and repeatedly, to give themselves in faithful love.
That does not make sexual intimacy optional or insignificant.
Paul clearly treats it as important.
But importance does not create permission for coercion.
Marriage creates profound obligations of fidelity, care, honesty, affection, and mutual sexual responsibility.
It does not transform a spouse into property.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this without theological fog:
A wedding ring does not make cruelty holy.
Sexual coercion does not become Christlike because the coercing person can quote Scripture.
At the same time, perhaps someone else needs to hear this:
If you have been deliberately using sexual rejection to punish, control, bargain with, or humiliate your spouse, do not hide behind therapeutic language while refusing conviction.
Bring that before Jesus too.
Repentance belongs on both sides of selfishness.
The goal is not to discover which spouse can weaponize the better verse.
The goal is transformation.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus walks into places we have made ugly.
Places stained by selfishness.
Places damaged by lust.
Places poisoned by resentment.
Places carrying sexual shame.
Places where Scripture itself may have been misused.
And He does not merely say, “Try harder.”
He calls sinners to repentance and offers sinners mercy.
The cross tells the truth about our sin without abandoning us to it.
Jesus does not excuse what destroys us.
He forgives, cleanses, restores, teaches, and transforms those who come to Him.
Maybe you have pressured someone you claimed to love.
Repent.
Not performatively.
Not with “I'm sorry you felt pressured.”
Own it.
Confess it.
Seek forgiveness.
Change.
Learn patience.
Become safe.
Maybe you have used affection as currency.
Repent.
Maybe pornography has distorted your expectations until your spouse feels like a failed performer instead of a beloved person made in God's image.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe betrayal shattered the trust that once made intimacy easy.
Healing may require more than telling the wounded spouse to “obey 1 Corinthians 7.”
Trust that took seconds to destroy may require a long season to rebuild.
Maybe you are the wounded spouse.
What happened to you does not become righteous merely because someone attached God's name to it.
Jesus is not honored when Scripture is twisted into permission for selfishness.

And if you are presently in a situation involving sexual violence, coercion, threats, or abuse, seeking safety and appropriate outside help is not a betrayal of biblical marriage. Serious abuse should not be concealed behind Christian vocabulary.
The church must become a place where people can tell the truth.
Not a place where victims are handed verses designed to silence them.
Not a place where selfish spouses are affirmed in entitlement.
And not a place where biblical teaching about marital intimacy is abandoned because speaking about sex makes everyone uncomfortable.
We need the whole truth.
Sex matters.
Mutuality matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Consent and agreement matter.
Self-control matters.
Compassion matters.
Repentance matters.
Marriage matters.
And above everything, Christ matters.
Because 1 Corinthians 7:5 is ultimately not permission to become more selfish.
Properly read in its context, it confronts selfishness.
“Do not deprive one another.”
One another.
There it is again.
Not domination.
Reciprocity.
Not exploitation.
Mutual responsibility.
Not “How can I use Scripture to make you give me what I want?”
But:
“How can we belong faithfully to one another while both belonging ultimately to Christ?”
Maybe that is the conversation Christian marriages desperately need.
Not merely:
“How often should married Christians have sex?”
But:
“Do you feel loved by me?”
“Do you feel safe telling me the truth?”
“Have I been selfish?”
“Have I been withholding?”
“Have I pressured you?”
“Have I stopped listening?”
“Is there pain I haven't noticed?”
“What do I need to confess?”
“How can we rebuild what has been damaged?”
And perhaps the hardest question:
“Am I trying to make you serve my desires, or am I learning to love you like Jesus?”
Do not answer too quickly.
Sit with it.
Because sometimes the verse we thought gave us ammunition turns around and places us on the witness stand.
That is what Scripture does.
It reads us while we are reading it.
And when it exposes us, grace does not tell us to run.
Grace tells us where to run.
Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to give strangers the details of your marriage. But do not keep hiding from Christ.
Sometimes another wounded believer needs to see that sentence and realize they are not the only one.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable, but because one day you may need to return to the difference between biblical mutuality and selfish entitlement.

Sharing biblical truth is one simple way to help it reach a marriage, a wounded believer, a struggling Christian, or even someone who has walked away from church because Scripture was once used against them.
Some truths should be shared publicly; some wounds deserve privacy and tenderness.
It does not.
They do not.

Christians hold differing convictions about how Old Testament tithing relates to New Testament giving, while the New Testament explicitly emphasizes willing, cheerful generosity rather than giving “under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So let your support come freely.
And there is another way to help that costs nothing.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Save what strengthens you.
Share what may rescue someone from a lie.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession becomes the first crack through which light enters.
Above all, follow Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about winning an argument in the bedroom.
It is about sinners being transformed into people who increasingly resemble the Savior who gave Himself for them.
And maybe that is the line worth carrying with you tonight:
Never use the hands Jesus died to redeem to grasp what Christ is teaching you to give in love.
